question: In an overparameterized deep linear regression model whose equivalent global minima span arbitrarily different parameter-space curvature, which sharpness is selected by the small-step, minibatch-SGD effective objective, and how does multi-output label-noise anisotropy change that selection?

key_findings.claim: Deep linear rescaling symmetries make functionally identical global minima arbitrarily sharp under the paper's Hessian-trace metric.
key_findings.evidence: For f(x)=W_D...W_1x, inserting any invertible A between adjacent factors leaves the function unchanged. Lemma 1 generalizes the familiar scalar rescaling argument to exponential symmetries, and the D=2 example gives T(W_2,W_1)=||W_2||_F^2 Tr Sigma_x+d_y Tr(W_1^T W_1 Sigma_x), which diverges along (lambda W_2, lambda^-1 W_1) while the loss is constant.

key_findings.claim: The central selection principle is minimization of gradient fluctuation on the ordinary-loss minimizer manifold, not direct minimization of Hessian sharpness.
key_findings.evidence: The paper adopts the small-learning-rate entropic objective F_eta=E loss+(eta/4) E_B ||E_B gradient loss||^2. Its perturbation lemma says that a convergent sequence of global minimizers as eta approaches zero minimizes the fluctuation functional S over the base-loss minimizer manifold. Full-batch GD has zero batch-gradient term at an optimum, whereas minibatch gradients retain residual fluctuations that can balance factor rescalings.

anchors.section: A.2 Formal statement of the perturbation lemma

key_findings.claim: The paper exactly solves the minimizer of a leading-order effective objective, not the stochastic training trajectory advertised by the broadest wording.
key_findings.evidence: No SGD recurrence is solved. Lemma 2 is an eta-to-zero perturbation statement about global minimizers of F_eta, conditional on convergence, and Theorem 1 imports a characterization of those balanced minimizers. The authors explicitly concede that the theory is effective rather than dynamical, covers only the leading order in eta, assumes stable small-step training, and cannot explain edge-of-stability behavior. Thus initialization-independent SGD convergence and the time path to the selected solution remain empirical hypotheses.

key_findings.claim: Within the full-rank, sufficiently wide deep-linear model, Theorem 1 gives a unique selected Hessian spectrum and closed-form trace even though the unregularized minimizer manifold contains every sharpness above a finite lower bound.
key_findings.evidence: Let V'=sqrt(Sigma_epsilon) V sqrt(Sigma_x)=L S R and require the bottleneck width at least rank(V'). Equations 14-15 give the selected trace and the minimum possible trace. Lemma 5 expresses every selected factor through the singular directions and arbitrary internal semi-orthogonal frames; Appendix A.3 shows those frames act by orthogonal similarity on the Hessian, preserving its spectrum. The minimum trace follows from an AM-GM and nuclear-norm factorization bound in Lemma 4.

key_findings.claim: For full-rank problems the selected trace can grow between square-root and linear order in the label-noise covariance condition number, and the two-output isotropic-teacher example approaches a square-root-in-condition-number excess.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary 1 bounds the selected trace between c_1 D sqrt(kappa(Sigma_epsilon)) and c_2 D kappa(Sigma_epsilon). With Sigma_x=V=I and Sigma_epsilon=diag(1,sigma^2), the paper obtains a symmetric expression minimized at sigma=1 and T/T_min approximately max(sigma,sigma^-1)=sqrt(kappa) for deep, highly imbalanced cases. The commuting-matrix result gives analogous bounds for the maximum Hessian eigenvalue.

anchors.section: Noise Imbalance as a Source of Sharpness; Corollaries 1-2
Largest Eigenvalue Has a Similar Property; Corollary 3

key_findings.claim: The manuscript contradicts itself about the sign of the condition-number effect.
key_findings.evidence: The contribution list on page 2 says converged sharpness is 'inversely proportional' to the condition number of Sigma_epsilon. The abstract, Corollary 1, Equations 18-22, all experiments, and the conclusion instead say and show that sharpness increases with imbalance/condition number. This appears to be a consequential wording error rather than an alternative convention.

key_findings.claim: The general fluctuation-versus-sharpness inequality in Theorem 2 is reversed as written.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 29-30 define T=Tr A and S=Tr(Sigma_epsilon A) for the positive-semidefinite matrix A=E[J J^T]. The elementary eigenvalue bound is lambda_min(Sigma_epsilon) T <= S <= lambda_max(Sigma_epsilon) T, equivalently S/lambda_max <= T <= S/lambda_min. Theorem 2 instead prints lambda_min S <= T <= lambda_max S. For isotropic Sigma_epsilon=cI, the definitions give S=cT, while the printed theorem would require c^2 T <= T <= c^2 T and fails whenever c is not one. This error affects the general-theory exposition, though Theorem 1 is derived separately from explicit deep-linear formulas.

key_findings.claim: The formal 'flattest if and only if Sigma_epsilon=I' corollary is too narrow; every positive scalar multiple of the identity yields the same fluctuation-minimizing and trace-minimizing factors.
key_findings.evidence: If Sigma_epsilon=cI, then S_fluctuation=c T at a well-specified MSE optimum, so minimizing either functional selects the same factors for any c>0. The paper's own isotropic experiments use sqrt(Sigma_epsilon)=diag(10,10), hence Sigma_epsilon=100I, and show convergence to the minimum-sharpness line. Appendix A.7 proves only the normalized c=1 substitution and never states a trace or scale normalization that would make 'only if I' literal.

key_findings.claim: Several distributional assumptions needed to reduce the population objective and fluctuation to Sigma_x and Sigma_epsilon are unstated in the model section.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 states only E[x]=0 and E[epsilon]=0 before asserting that global minima implement Vx for every training x. For population MSE this requires at least zero conditional mean or E[epsilon x^T]=0 plus sufficient input support; for the fluctuation factorization into separate input and residual covariances, a stronger second-moment independence condition is needed. Theorem 2 later explicitly assumes residual independence, revealing the missing bridge. For a finite noisy training set, Equation 5 is generally false without interpolation/repeated-noise qualifications.

key_findings.claim: The perturbation lemma's stated coercivity premise conflicts with the rescaling-symmetric deep-linear loss to which it is applied.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix Lemma 3 assumes the base loss f is coercive so its minimizer set is compact and a convergent subsequence exists. Yet Sections 3.1-3.2 explicitly exhibit unbounded rescaling paths with exactly constant loss, so the deep-linear f is not coercive and its minimizer manifold is noncompact. The lemma's algebra remains valid conditional on a convergent sequence, but the paper does not separately establish existence, boundedness, or convergence of global F_eta minimizers as eta approaches zero in the stated model.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic SGD experiments qualitatively support anisotropy-driven sharpening and show that switching to full-batch GD arrests the continuing drift.
key_findings.evidence: In the D=3, two-dimensional linear problem, online SGD with sqrt(Sigma_epsilon)=diag(10,0.1) increases Hessian trace and top eigenvalue far above the isotropic diag(10,10) runs, while isotropic runs approach the analytic minimum. Five-run ReLU teacher-student and noisy-soft-label MNIST experiments show the same sign. In Figure 4, switching the anisotropic linear run from batch-10 SGD to batch-1000 GD at step 20,000 freezes sharpness near the switch value while continued SGD keeps rising; full-batch GD alone remains near the minimum.

key_findings.claim: The nonlinear, RNN, and Transformer results are qualitative stress tests under artificial noise, not evidence that the exact mechanism governs realistic deep learning or language-model token entropy.
key_findings.evidence: The only Transformer is one two-head attention layer plus a residual MLP on Gaussian sequences of length four and dimension eight, with a width-100 teacher and width-4 student. The RNN uses the same tiny teacher-student regime. MNIST noise is created by adding Gaussian noise to one-hot labels and applying softmax, not by natural annotation noise. The condition-number sweep lowers smaller noise eigenvalues while fixing the largest, changing total variance and SNR; it lacks trace-matched spectra, eigenvector permutations, or convergence-to-global-minimum checks. Cross-entropy results are outside the MSE theorem, and the stopword/content-word explanation is not tested on a language model.

key_findings.claim: The empirical condition-number sweep does not verify the theory's asymptotic scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 reports monotonic relative trace but plateaus by condition number 10^2-10^3: the MSE linear curve is below 5 even at kappa=10^5, whereas the illustrative asymptotic predicts approximately sqrt(kappa). Cross-entropy MLP and RNN curves rise only to about 1.1. The authors attribute saturation to finite training horizon without supplying longer-horizon convergence, fitted exponents, or uncertainty bars. The plots therefore establish direction of association in these setups, not the derived kappa law or arbitrary-sharpness limit.

key_findings.claim: The work separates the selected parameter-space curvature from initialization-dependent trajectory direction, but it does not connect either quantity to generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 derives expected initial trace for Gaussian, Xavier, and Kaiming initialization; Figure 1 shows small initialization sharpens and large initialization flattens toward a similar level. However, all empirical endpoints are curvature measures. No held-out loss, accuracy-versus-sharpness analysis, function-space flatness, or reparameterization-invariant generalization metric is reported, despite the introduction motivating flatness through generalization.

method.core_idea: Use a deep linear factorization with a continuum of functionally equivalent curvature levels, replace small-step minibatch SGD by its leading-order entropic objective, and solve exactly which factor balancing minimizes stochastic gradient fluctuation under multi-output label noise.
method.mechanism: A linear teacher y=Vx+epsilon supplies input covariance Sigma_x and output-noise covariance Sigma_epsilon. Matrix rescaling makes the ordinary global-minimum manifold noncompact and arbitrarily sharp. The entropic objective adds expected squared minibatch-gradient magnitude; as eta tends to zero, the selected point is characterized as the minimum-fluctuation point on that manifold. An SVD of sqrt(Sigma_epsilon) V sqrt(Sigma_x) yields closed-form layer factors, Hessian trace, minimum attainable trace, condition-number bounds, and, under covariance/singular-vector alignment, a closed-form top Hessian eigenvalue. Simulations compare isotropic and anisotropic noise in deep linear, ReLU, RNN, tiny Transformer, and MNIST settings and intervene by switching SGD to GD.
assumptions: Training is accurately represented by the leading-order entropic objective for small positive learning rate and stable minibatch dynamics.
A sequence of global entropic-objective minimizers exists, remains bounded, and converges as eta approaches zero.
The population residual has zero conditional mean relative to x and the moments needed to factor input and noise covariances are independent.
The input covariance and label-noise covariance are positive definite where inverses and condition numbers are used.
Every hidden bottleneck width is at least rank(sqrt(Sigma_epsilon) V sqrt(Sigma_x)).
Training reaches the relevant global optimum rather than a different stationary point or a nonstationary distribution.
Hessian trace is an appropriate, parameterization-specific sharpness proxy for the question of factor selection.
The maximum-eigenvalue formula additionally requires covariance eigenvectors to align/commute with teacher singular vectors.
Finite-horizon synthetic SGD has run long enough to approximate the predicted equilibrium.
Artificial Gaussian soft-label noise and tiny teacher-student models preserve the mechanism outside linear MSE.

techniques.role: Creates functionally identical deep-linear solutions spanning unbounded Hessian sharpness.
Provides an exactly tractable curvature functional and a coarse link to the top Hessian eigenvalue.
Represents leading-order discrete/minibatch SGD bias as base loss plus expected squared batch-gradient fluctuation.
Selects among base-loss minimizers by minimizing residual stochastic gradient magnitude.
Diagonalizes sqrt(Sigma_epsilon) V sqrt(Sigma_x) to express selected layer factors and curvature.
Uses AM-GM and Schatten norm inequalities to derive the minimum trace over all exact factorizations.
Shows arbitrary internal selected frames change the Hessian only by orthogonal similarity.
Bounds selected trace and, under alignment, top eigenvalue between square-root and linear dependence on noise anisotropy.
Tests whether continued stochasticity is necessary for post-convergence sharpening drift.
Approximates nonlinear-model Hessian trace where exact computation is impractical.
Estimates the largest Hessian eigenvalue in empirical checks.

evaluations.setting: Three-layer linear network, d_x=d_y=2, V=I, standard-Gaussian x; sqrt noise covariance diag(10,0.1) versus diag(10,10); online SGD for 100,000 epochs, learning rate 0.01, batch 10, five trials.
evaluations.metric: Exact Hessian trace and power-method top eigenvalue on 200 random samples over training.
evaluations.result: Anisotropic runs progressively rise to much larger trace and top eigenvalue, while isotropic runs stay close to the analytic minimum-sharpness line; the curves remain noisy and finite-horizon.
evaluations.baseline: Isotropic noise and the closed-form minimum trace/top-eigenvalue prediction.

evaluations.setting: Same anisotropic linear system with learning rate 0.001; batch-10 SGD switched at step 20,000 to batch-1000 GD.
evaluations.metric: Hessian-trace trajectory after the optimizer switch.
evaluations.result: The switched run remains near its approximately 85-at-switch curvature while uninterrupted SGD continues toward roughly 120; GD from initialization remains near the roughly 25 minimum. The intervention shows stochastic updates are needed for continued drift, not that GD returns an already-sharp factorization to the flattest one.
evaluations.baseline: Uninterrupted SGD, uninterrupted batch-1000 GD, and minimum-sharpness line.

evaluations.setting: Single-hidden-layer ReLU teacher-student regression, d_x=d_y=2, width-100 teacher/width-4 student, sqrt noise scales diag(3,0.03) versus diag(3,3), 100,000 epochs, learning rate 0.1, batch 100, five trials.
evaluations.metric: Hutchinson Hessian trace and top Hessian eigenvalue on 200 samples.
evaluations.result: Anisotropic noise yields a gradual, modestly sharper endpoint than isotropic noise in both measures, qualitatively matching the predicted sign but not testing the deep-linear formula.
evaluations.baseline: Isotropic noise under otherwise shared hyperparameters.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer 128-hidden-unit ReLU network on MNIST with cross-entropy; Gaussian perturbation of one-hot labels followed by softmax; sqrt covariance with five entries 10 and five entries 1 versus 10I; 10,000 epochs, learning rate 0.01, batch 128, five trials.
evaluations.metric: Hessian trace and top eigenvalue on a 1,024-example test batch.
evaluations.result: The anisotropic condition is visibly sharper throughout most training, but total injected noise power and class-direction assignment are not matched and no predictive performance is reported.

evaluations.setting: MSE and cross-entropy condition-number sweeps for linear, MLP, RNN, and tiny Transformer teacher-student models.
evaluations.metric: Relative sharpness: anisotropic Hessian trace divided by the isotropic trace.
evaluations.result: All plotted curves are monotone before plateauing, but MSE endpoints range only about 1.7-4.8 and cross-entropy MLP/RNN endpoints are about 1.1; no fitted kappa exponent, seed uncertainty, trace-matched spectrum, or equilibrium verification is supplied.
evaluations.baseline: Condition number one/isotropic label covariance within each architecture and loss.

evaluations.setting: One-layer two-head Transformer with residual MLP, input/output dimension 8, sequence length 4, teacher/student MLP widths 100/4; Gaussian regression; sqrt covariance diag(4,0.04,...,0.04) versus diag(4,...,4); 10,000 epochs, learning rate 0.03, batch 300.
evaluations.metric: Hessian trace and top eigenvalue on 1,000 test samples.
evaluations.result: Anisotropic curves rise above isotropic curves, reaching visually about 90 versus 45 in trace and 6.3 versus 4.2 in top eigenvalue. This supports qualitative transfer to a toy attention block, not a modern language model.

evaluations.setting: Linear-network appendix sweeps over depth two, three, and four and tracks layer condition numbers for balanced versus imbalanced output noise.
evaluations.metric: Trace/depth, top eigenvalue/depth, and per-layer weight condition number over 100,000 epochs.
evaluations.result: Depth-normalized curves are broadly comparable and anisotropic noise preferentially increases first/last factor condition numbers; finite-horizon curves have not reached the extreme covariance condition number used in the data.

evaluations.metric: Trajectory theorem, assumption closure, algebraic consistency, noise-scale matching, realistic architecture/data, generalization, and uncertainty.
evaluations.result: The exact contribution is an equilibrium of a leading-order effective objective; Theorem 2's inequality is reversed, Corollary 2 omits scalar-isotropic covariance, the perturbation lemma's coercivity does not hold for the target loss, empirical spectra change total variance, and no realistic Transformer or generalization outcome is tested.
evaluations.baseline: A decisive validation would simulate the theorem's exact factor equilibrium across eta and batch size, hold noise trace fixed while varying anisotropy/eigenbasis, report convergence residuals and seeds, and test modern networks plus held-out performance.

limitations: Author-stated: the theory is effective/equilibrium-based and does not solve the dynamics by which SGD reaches a sharper or flatter factorization.
Author-stated: only the leading-order effect in learning rate is modeled, so larger-step higher-order terms are unresolved.
Author-stated: the stable small-step derivation cannot explain edge-of-stability or edge-of-stochastic-stability behavior.
Reviewer-identified: the exact theorem is limited to sufficiently wide deep linear MSE regression with full-rank covariance conditions and an assumed global solution.
Reviewer-identified mathematical error: Theorem 2 reverses the eigenvalue inequality relating T=Tr A and S=Tr(Sigma_epsilon A).
Reviewer-identified mathematical error: 'flattest iff Sigma_epsilon=I' should at minimum include every cI, c>0; the paper's own isotropic experiment uses 100I.
Reviewer-identified contradiction: page 2 says sharpness is inversely proportional to noise condition number, opposite to the theorem, experiments, abstract, and conclusion.

Reviewer-identified proof gap: the formal perturbation lemma assumes a coercive base loss, but the deep-linear loss is noncoercive along the paper's rescaling symmetry; bounded convergence of F_eta minimizers is not separately proved.

Reviewer-identified assumption gap: zero-mean x and epsilon alone do not justify Equation 5 or covariance factorization; conditional-mean/independence and input-support assumptions are missing in Section 3.1.

Reviewer-identified notation/scope issue: the trace-to-top-eigenvalue bound uses d ambiguously and requires a positive-semidefinite Hessian; trace is not a universal stability proxy away from the analyzed MSE minima.
Reviewer-identified empirical confound: condition-number sweeps fix the largest noise eigenvalue and shrink others, changing total variance and signal-to-noise ratio rather than isolating anisotropy.

Reviewer-identified empirical gap: nonlinear and cross-entropy experiments lack a theorem, convergence diagnostics, trace-matched noise controls, eigenbasis permutations, and quantitative scaling fits.
Reviewer-identified scale gap: the Transformer has one two-head block, sequence length four, dimension eight, and Gaussian teacher-student data; no language model is trained or evaluated.
Reviewer-identified measurement gap: no held-out performance or generalization metric is related to curvature, despite generalization motivating the sharpness discussion.

Reviewer-identified statistical gap: only some figures specify five trials and standard errors; Figure 3's condition-number curves show no uncertainty or fit sensitivity, and Hessian-estimator probe counts are incomplete.
Reviewer-identified extrapolation gap: stopword/content-word entropy is not an input-independent additive output-noise covariance, so the proposed language-model explanation is speculative.
failure_modes: Finite-step SGD can enter edge-of-stability dynamics where higher-order curvature forces dominate the leading-order fluctuation objective.
Noncompact factor rescalings can prevent convergence of the global-minimizer sequence assumed by the perturbation lemma.
Correlated or heteroscedastic residuals make a single, input-independent Sigma_epsilon insufficient to predict factor selection.
Rank-deficient teacher maps or noise covariances invalidate inverses, condition numbers, and the claimed if-and-only-if statement.
Optimization can stop at a non-global stationary point or stationary distribution whose sharpness depends on initialization and finite eta.
Changing noise condition number while changing its trace can make a nonlinear model sharpen because of SNR or target-scale effects rather than anisotropy.
Cross-entropy classification can have a label Hessian and residual structure that do not reduce to the MSE covariance mechanism.
Parameter-space rescaling can change trace and top eigenvalue without changing the learned function or generalization, making sharpness comparisons operationally misleading.
A finite training horizon can create apparent plateaus far below the predicted equilibrium and obscure the claimed arbitrary-sharpness scaling.
Switching to GD can merely freeze the current rescaling coordinate rather than reveal an opposing flatness-seeking bias.
Toy Transformer behavior may disappear with normalization, attention depth, vocabulary cross-entropy, adaptive optimization, or real token distributions.
reusable_insights: Separate the irreducible minimum curvature required by task/architecture from optimizer-selected excess curvature along function-preserving symmetries.
Gradient-fluctuation minimization and Hessian-trace minimization coincide only under isotropic residual covariance; anisotropic weighting can prefer a sharper parameterization.
Multi-output covariance is a genuine degree of freedom hidden by scalar-output analyses, where every positive variance is automatically isotropic.
Optimizer-switch interventions can distinguish continuing stochastic drift from landscape-driven sharpening, but should be paired with reverse switches and state-matched controls.
An exact equilibrium formula should be tested with convergence residuals and predicted scaling, not only qualitative trajectory separation.
When varying covariance anisotropy, hold trace, determinant, marginal SNR, and eigenbasis controls fixed separately.
Check the domain assumptions of generic perturbation lemmas against neural-network symmetry manifolds; coercivity frequently fails exactly where implicit-bias questions are interesting.
Keep trace sharpness, top-eigenvalue stability, function-space sensitivity, and generalization as distinct outcomes.
For A positive semidefinite, remember lambda_min(Sigma) Tr A <= Tr(Sigma A) <= lambda_max(Sigma) Tr A; inversion is required when bounding Tr A from the weighted trace.
open_questions: Can the selected factorization be derived directly from the SGD recurrence with finite eta, batch size, and a nonasymptotic convergence time?
Does a corrected, fully stated theorem hold for heteroscedastic residual covariance Sigma_epsilon(x) or correlated x and epsilon?
Can the coercivity mismatch be repaired by quotienting rescaling symmetries or proving the fluctuation term makes F_eta equicoercive?
What are the finite-eta corrections to the selected trace, and when do they reverse the small-step anisotropy effect?
Do trace-matched anisotropic spectra cause sharpening in normalized deep networks and realistic cross-entropy tasks?
How do adaptive optimizers, momentum, weight decay, batch normalization, and RMSNorm alter the covariance-conditioned equilibrium?
Does anisotropy-selected parameter sharpness predict any function-space robustness or held-out generalization after controlling for reparameterization?
Can realistic language-model residuals be estimated as output-space covariance operators, and do their spectra predict layer-factor sharpness?
How does this small-step mechanism interact with the later stochastic self-stabilization mechanism at the edge of stability?

competitive_landscape.title: Parameter Symmetry and Noise Equilibrium of Stochastic Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziyin et al. already prove noise-driven motion along exponential symmetries to initialization-independent equilibria and explicitly use it to explain progressive sharpening/flattening. The present paper specializes that mechanism to multi-output deep linear regression and derives an exact covariance-conditioned trace and spectrum.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Thermodynamics: Entropic Forces in Deep and Universal Representation Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Ziyin, Xu, and Chuang develop the entropic-force framework and balanced-factor characterization reused as Lemma 5, and already claim to reconcile flatness- and sharpness-seeking behavior. The new contribution is the explicit label-noise-spectrum solution and sharpness bounds for one solvable model, not the minimum-fluctuation principle itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Label Noise SGD Provably Prefers Flat Global Minimizers
competitive_landscape.difference: Damian, Ma, and Lee derive a label-noise-induced regularizer that penalizes sharp minima, with convergence, large-learning-rate, momentum, classification, and general-covariance extensions. The present result identifies a multi-output anisotropic regime where minimizing a different fluctuation functional can instead select a sharper factorization; reconciling the noise models and asymptotic regimes is essential to the claimed reversal.

competitive_landscape.title: What Happens after SGD Reaches Zero Loss? --A Mathematical Framework
competitive_landscape.difference: Li, Wang, and Arora derive a long-timescale SDE on a minimizer manifold with arbitrary noise covariance, directly addressing post-convergence dynamics. The present paper offers a closed-form endpoint for a richer multi-output factorization but assumes the effective-objective minimizer rather than proving the SGD path reaches it.

competitive_landscape.title: Sharpness of Minima in Deep Matrix Factorization
competitive_landscape.difference: Kamber and Parhi give an exact top-Hessian-eigenvalue expression at arbitrary deep-matrix-factorization minimizers and characterize spectral-norm balancing for flatness. The present paper cites the concurrent formula, focuses mainly on trace, and adds which minimizer a covariance-weighted SGD effective objective selects.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep linear networks for regression are implicitly regularized towards flat minima
competitive_landscape.difference: Marion and Chizat prove that gradient flow selects near-minimal top-eigenvalue sharpness in univariate deep-linear regression under specific initializations. The present model is multi-output and stochastic, exposing label-noise anisotropy that is impossible in a scalar output, but its trajectory guarantee is weaker.

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Converges Linearly to Flatter Minima than Gradient Flow in Shallow Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Beneventano and Woodworth solve finite-step GD dynamics in a scalar depth-2 network and find large-step discretization selects flatter solutions than gradient flow. The present mechanism is minibatch-noise conditioned and can select sharper solutions, emphasizing that deterministic step-size and stochastic covariance biases need not agree.

competitive_landscape.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: Andreyev and Beneventano show that minibatch SGD stabilizes batch sharpness rather than the full-batch top Hessian eigenvalue and that smaller batches can suppress lambda_max. This is a different, large-step stability regime that the present small-eta effective theory explicitly cannot cover and that pushes sharpness in the opposite direction.

competitive_landscape.title: SGD at the Edge of Stability: The Stochastic Sharpness Gap
competitive_landscape.difference: Liao et al. derive a stochastic self-stabilization coupling and a closed-form noise-dependent reduction in equilibrium top-eigenvalue sharpness at the edge of stability. This later result reinforces that gradient noise can flatten in a finite-step regime, bounding any broad reading that anisotropic noise generally makes SGD seek sharpness.

competitive_landscape.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
competitive_landscape.difference: Dinh et al. establish that function-preserving symmetries can make parameter-space minima arbitrarily sharp without changing generalization. The present paper productively uses the same issue as a selection manifold, but its trace outcome remains parameterization-specific and cannot support a generalization claim without an invariant metric.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first exactly solvable model in which SGD's implicit bias can select either flatness or arbitrary sharpness, with the output label-noise spectrum uniquely determining the converged curvature through minimum gradient fluctuation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form selected Hessian trace and invariant selected spectrum for a multi-output deep-linear model; Corollaries 1-3 link trace and top eigenvalue to noise condition number; controlled SGD, optimizer-switch, nonlinear, RNN, MNIST, and tiny-Transformer experiments reproduce the qualitative sign.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The genuinely new core is the explicit multi-output covariance-conditioned solution and its demonstration that a minimum-fluctuation equilibrium need not be the minimum-trace factorization. The surrounding ingredients—arbitrarily sharp symmetry orbits, noise equilibria, the entropic objective, balanced deep-linear factors, exact deep-matrix-factorization sharpness, and both flatness- and sharpening mechanisms—have direct priority. The broad 'exactly solving SGD' and realistic-architecture implications overstate an effective small-eta endpoint, and the reversed Theorem 2 inequality, scalar-isotropy omission, coercivity mismatch, and inverse/direct-condition-number contradiction require correction before treating the theoretical package as fully established.

Provenance was independently checked on 2026-08-23: local PDF/text SHA-256 values exactly match fulltext_index.jsonl, all 25 pages contain extractable text, and a fresh explicit download of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.05065v1 matched PDF SHA-256 3ebd1c2fa78fad97a2cb05259db67044316f6a0ee8f73088f9aeeb8c60915634. The arXiv record remains v1. Proof audit re-derived the trace/fluctuation matrix inequality and scalar-isotropic special case, checked the perturbation lemma's premises against the paper's noncompact rescaling orbit, and traced the condition-number sign through the introduction, corollaries, and plots; the longer algebraic factor formulas were consistency-read but not independently machine-verified. Competitor searches covered covariance/noise mechanism, deep-linear exact sharpness and baselines, and the paper's novelty language plus cited predecessors; all ten primary arXiv records were opened and version-pinned on 2026-08-23. Confidence is high for the paper's stated model, equations, plots, and identified formal contradictions, but calibrated below verification because no second reviewer or executable author artifact was used. This remains full_text, not verified.
